title: Pathway latency diagnostics — labbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a working labbook capturing a focused set of E2E trace experiments run against the current canary of the serving runtime (sha: canary-2026-02-17). Goal is to understand recent p95/p99 volatility and isolate the stage-level contributors so we can propose targeted mitigations for the next sprint.

Summary of top-level finding (short):
- Observed sustained p50 ~ 48 ms, p95 ~ 260 ms, p99 ~ 1,050 ms for short-sequence traffic (seq_len <= 32) during mid-day traffic bursts.
- The p99 tail is dominated by two phenomena: long batching wait states (queue dwell) and intermittent kernel coldstarts on GPU workers (kernel-init spikes).
- KV cache lookups (for prefix caching) reduce average cost but occasionally add large variance when cache-miss amplification intersects with batching windows.

High-level trace methodology and sampling notes:
- Traces were captured with the sampling harness attached to canary probe endpoints across three regions (us-east1, europe-west1, ap-southeast1).
- Sampling rules: 1% uniform sampling + targeted triggers for requests that exceed 350 ms (auto upsample).
- Instrumentation exported: ingress receive, auth & routing, model selection, preproc, KV cache op, batching enqueue, batching dequeue, forward-pass (kernel exec), kv-store writeback, postproc, egress send.
- Each span has seq_len, model_variant, worker_id, batch_size_at_submit, and kv_hit boolean.
- Important caveat: some short bursts were correlated with infra maintenance windows (noticed on 2026-02-29) — we exclude those intervals from the main aggregation.

Representative aggregated numbers (short sequnce traffic, seq_len<=32, N=184k requests over 48h):
- p50: 48 ms
- p75: 96 ms
- p90: 190 ms
- p95: 260 ms
- p99: 1,050 ms
- max observed: 3,120 ms (outlier tied to intermittent control-plane delay)

Per-stage median and tail contributions (stacked decomposition approach):
- Ingress receive & routing: median 6 ms, p95 14 ms, p99 55 ms (~5–7% of p99 total)
- Auth & model lookup: median 3 ms, p95 10 ms, p99 40 ms (~3–5%)
- KV cache op (lookup only): median 2 ms (hit), 18 ms (miss), p95 60 ms, p99 220 ms (~20% of p99 when miss-heavy)
- Batching queue wait (time in queue until batch threshold or timeout): median 8 ms, p95 120 ms, p99 680 ms (~55% of p99)
- Forward-pass (kernel exec): median 18 ms, p95 32 ms, p99 140 ms (~10–20%)
- Postprocess & egress: median 4 ms, p95 12 ms, p99 45 ms (~3–6%)

Key trace archetypes discovered:
1) Queue-dominated tail (most common at p99): batch waiting produced long dwell due to sporadic microbursts. Traces show single-request batches held for ~650–900 ms waiting for either batch fill or timeout because adaptive-batcher thresholds were tuned too aggressively for cost.
2) Cache-miss cascade: request hits a KV-miss that triggers a small retrieval job (fusion with remote store) which in a subset of workers experiences additional queueing and adds ~150–300 ms. Often co-occurs with batch-wait.
3) Kernel init jitter: rare but high-impact where a worker that had been idle for >30s experienced kernel launch or CUDA context init latency (~300–2,000 ms depending on GC state). Correlated with worker churn observed in node metrics.
4) Egress backpressure: downstream client connection slowdowns caused TLS send stalls visible in traces, adding ~100–400 ms in some long traces (not dominant but noticeable).

Micro-observations and notes:
- Batch thresholding: the adaptive batch window currently uses throughput-driven heuristics that err on reducing latency by setting smaller timeouts at lower qps, but under bursty traffic this causes the system to wait for fill which paradoxically increases p99.
- Worker affinity: sticky routing to warmed workers reduces cold kernel init but increases coupling where group-wide GC or eviction causes multiple simultaneous kernel inits.
- KV store hotspots: certain prompt prefixes have very high cache churn; when those prefixes have a miss it creates a concentrated load on a small set of cache backends.

Immediate remediation proposals (short-term, quick win):
- Reduce max batch timeout from 1s -> 250ms for short-seq routes (config flag rollout canary). Expected p99 reduction ~300–500 ms in queue-dominated traces, tradeoff +6–10% in tokens-per-second efficiency.
- Pin a tiny warm-pool of workers for short-seq latency-critical routes (reserve 3 per AZ). This should eliminate the kernel-init class for those routes.
- Introduce a KV-miss de-dup window (100 ms) for identical prefix keys to collapse hotspot fan-out on the backend.

Medium-term platform changes to explore:
- Sequence-length aware batching policy that has different timeouts per seq_len bucket and dynamic migration when load changes.
- Per-worker lazy-context warmers: keep minimal CUDA contexts alive for N seconds after last use instead of full GC. Tunable by memory pressure.
- Enhanced trace-driven autoscaler: scale up temporary burst replicas when queue-dwell percentile crosses threshold.

Action items and owners (next 2 sprints):
- (ENG-3421) Implement short-route timeout change (owner: Ravi Anand) — target canary rollout by 2026-03-10.
- (ENG-3437) KV-miss de-dup patch and backend metric to measure collapse rate (owner: Maeve O'Connor) — experiment by 2026-03-17.
- (ENG-3445) Warm-pool config and operator flag for short-seq routes (owner: Lina Park) — design doc due 2026-03-09.
- Trace infra: add worker-level kernel-init tag and a dedicated counter to the metrics pipeline (owner: Jonas Meyer) — quick PR queued: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1142.

Remaining unknowns / follow-ups:
- Need to quantify cost impact (tokens/sec vs latency) precisely — run A/B for 72h after timeout change.
- Verify interaction between warm-pool and dedicated capacity customers (no noisy neighbor regressions).
- More sampling during night windows to confirm that kernel-init class is not masked by low daytime churn.

Appendix: quick trace examples (redacted)
- Trace A (queue-dominated p99): seq_len=8, kv_hit=true, batch_size_at_submit=1 -> queue_wait=762 ms, kernel_exec=22 ms, total=810 ms
- Trace B (kernel-init): seq_len=24, kv_hit=false, batch_size_at_submit=4 -> queue_wait=18 ms, kernel_init=1180 ms, kernel_exec=30 ms, total=1,250 ms
- Trace C (cache-miss cascade): seq_len=12, kv_hit=false, batch_size_at_submit=2 -> queue_wait=120 ms, kv_retrieval=210 ms, kernel_exec=28 ms, total=380 ms

Notes to self:
- Keep the labbook chronological: snapshot instrumented config as of 2026-02-17, include raw trace ids in the secure bucket for postmortem if needed.
- Share a short one-pager for the platform on-call team summarizing the queued timeout change once canary metrics look good.

End of labbook entry for this experiment set.
